rv.q: If the story, fashioned by book writers Colin Escott and Floyd Mutrux, is elemental and often a bit awkward, the musical performances are not — a galvanizing collection of singers and musicians who deliver the songs with an explosive authority that really rocks the house.
Million Dollar Quartet, a show poised delicately at the halfway point between a musical and a revue, distills that revolutionary spirit and splashes it out as a dazzling, raucous spectacle.
1956 was a momentous year: the Suez crisis, the Hungarian revolution, Khruschev's denuniciation of Stalin.
The knockout performances keep the joint jumpin’ with great balls of fire.
There's a lot to like about this relatively scrappy variation on a familiar theme.
The musicianship sells this entertainment.
What makes 'Million Dollar Quartet' worth seeing is that it tells its story through the songs that Elvis, Jerry Lee, Carl and Johnny actually sang that night
The show works best when it stops trying to be a play and just lets the music do the talking.
But the performances themselves are merely adequate.

But one can't help wondering if the City of Sin would also be a better venue for this lightweight show, which closes with its quartet donning sparkly jackets better suited to Liberace than rock legends.
The musical has just enough of a compelling narrative to keep audiences hooked between numbers.
All told, you're better off staying home and taking some old records off the shelf.
When the curtain call is the most exciting part of a show, it's definitely a problem.
Like everything else in Million Dollar Quartet, it's at best a fool's-gold gimmick.
The amplification to arena volume shoehorned into a mere Broadway theater treats one’s eardrums as percussion instruments.

One day in December 1956, four future musical legends -- Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis and Carl Perkins -- happened to gather together for an impromptu jam session at the Memphis studio of Sun Records. Don't look for 'Million Dollar Quartet,' the new musical about this fortuitous event, to show what really happened that day.

Lovers of old school rock ‘n' roll will get a big bang out of "Million Dollar Quartet," a mighty slick jukebox musical powered by a dynamite song stack and dynamic portrayals of the four legends singing ‘em.
Whatever the case, it's one hell of a winner.
And this jukebox musical jumps off the charts whenever Levi Kreis, who plays Jerry Lee Lewis, dominates the stage with his wild jazzy piano playing and furious rock lyrics.
But I just don't get the appeal of watching them pretend to be iconic figures whose work I can hear and see at the press of a button.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actor in a Musical

cn.t: Critics find this energetic recreation of the legendary 1956 jam session works best when it lets the music speak, with strong performances (especially Levi Kreis as Jerry Lee Lewis) overcoming a thin storyline.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
